Title: A Remote Attestation Protocol Oriented to the SuperPOD Structure
Text:
A Remote Attestation Protocol Oriented to the SuperPOD
Structure
Jiajun Zhong∗
School of Cyber Science and Technology
University of Science and Technology of China
HeFei, Anhui, China
aetghost@mail.ustc.edu.cn
Abstract
With the rapid development of artificial intelligence and machine
learning in recent years, their complexity has also increased rapidly,
and therefore the demand for high-performance computing has also
increased rapidly. The traditional way of distributing training and
inference work to a large number of servers will further increase
the complexity of these tasks and slow down the process, which is
particularly detrimental to those tasks that are time-sensitive. To
solve these problems, many designs have emerged that integrate
a large number of GPUs together, such as the DGX SuperPOD
architecture launched by NVIDIA. However, as the number of GPUs
in a server increases, security issues also arise. It is obviously too
cumbersome to directly verify each GPU one by one. Therefore,
we can refer to the swarm attestation mechanism of IoT devices
and design a new remote attestation protocol based on structures
such as SuperPOD that integrate a large number of GPUs together,
so that users can quickly verify the security of a large number of
GPUs in the SuperPOD structure, thereby improving the efficiency
of remote attestation. This paper introduces the swarm attestation
mechanism of the Internet of Things into the remote attestation of
a multi-GPU cluster with a SuperPOD structure, proposes a remote
attestation protocol based on the swarm attestation mechanism, and
verifies in simulation that it is more efficient than simply expanding
the ordinary one-to-one GPU remote attestation mechanism. At
the same time, its analysis shows that the scheme can resist attacks
such as forgery and replay.

Introduction
In recent years, large language models have developed rapidly and
made great achievements in natural language processing, and have
produced world-renowned results such as Chat GPT. In addition,
large language models are also widely used in related traditional
natural language processing fields such as machine translation,
text summarization, reading comprehension, and many related
explorations in program analysis, code testing, code generation,
etc.
As large language models are used by more and more individuals
and enterprises, security issues related to large models are becoming
more and more important, and users are increasingly concerned
about security risks. As large models themselves develop rapidly,
so too are security threats related to large models. These threats are
mainly reflected in the security issues of large models themselves
(such as large models being attacked by poisoning with specific
data inserted), security issues of large models during training (such
as ensuring the security of labeled data and preventing the training
process itself from being attacked), security of large models during
the inference phase (such as accidental leakage of user input data
or the inference results containing privacy content that should
not appear), and the contradiction between the computing power
security and computing power utilization efficiency of large models.
Among them, the contradiction between computing power security
and computing power utilization efficiency will become more and
more significant as the scale of large models expands. The training
of large models itself requires a large amount of computing power
resources, so it is particularly important to ensure that they are not
abused or attacked during use.
In order to adapt to the requirements of computing power for
the development of large models, especially many large models
used in special occasions need to be trained in a targeted manner
(for example, large models that generate codes in different pro-
gramming languages need to be trained with a large amount of
code), computing power base providers have to continuously ex-
pand the computing power of nodes, and computing power node
models represented by NVIDIA SuperPOD have emerged, which
are characterized by the use of a large number of computing power
nodes to cope with the challenges of AI, high-performance com-
puting, and the combination of the above two requirements. In
these scenarios, users use the trusted computing services provided
by service providers on the cloud, rather than the costly form of

deploying a large number of devices locally, which in turn poses
new challenges to the security of large models. At present, in order
to ensure the trustworthiness and security of service providers,
users need to verify the security of computing nodes provided by
service providers through remote attestation protocols. Only after
ensuring the security of computing nodes can computing nodes on
the cloud be safely used to complete the training of large models.
At present, the superPOD model lacks excellent practices in the
field of remote attestation. If the traditional one-to-one remote at-
testation protocol is used, the large number of computing nodes in
the superPOD model will make the entire attestation process very
lengthy and waste resources. However, security verification of com-
puting nodes is an essential part of ensuring the security of large
models. However, there are already many related studies on remote
attestation schemes between a large number of nodes, especially
in the field of the Internet of Things. Remote attestation processes
involving a large number of devices are very common. Swarm
attestation is a type of remote attestation scheme that considers
a large number of IoT devices. However, these existing remote
attestation protocols are designed for the specific usage scenarios
of IoT devices and the limited performance of a single device, and
are not suitable for direct application in the superPOD model.
Therefore, this paper focuses on the swarm remote attestation
scheme for the superPOD mode, and proposes a GPU swarm re-
mote attestation mechanism that introduces the swarm attestation
mechanism into multiple host nodes. This paper introduces the
swarm attestation mechanism of the Internet of Things into the
remote attestation of a multi-GPU cluster with a SuperPOD struc-
ture, proposes a remote attestation protocol based on the swarm
attestation mechanism, and verifies in simulation that it is more
efficient than simply expanding the ordinary one-to-one[1,2,3,4,5]
remote attestation mechanism. At the same time, its analysis shows
that the scheme can resist attacks such as forgery and replay.
Section 2 of this paper first introduces the relevant research work
on the superPOD mode and swarm attestation; Section 3 introduces
the mechanism we proposed; Section 4 analyzes and evaluates
the efficiency of the proposed remote verification mechanism; and
finally summarizes the whole paper in the Section 5.
2
Related Work
2.1
SuperPOD Structure
Today, large model training is a task that requires a lot of computing
power. For example, GPT3 has hundreds of billions of parameters,
and GPT4 has trillions of parameters. They are a mixture of mul-
tiple expert models. Although OpenAI has not released relevant
information, according to various information available on the In-
ternet, it is estimated that GPT4 used about 25,000 A100 GPUs and
trained for 90 to 100 days, which is also an astonishing amount of
computing power.
The heavy large model training tasks are highly dependent on
high-performance computing. At present, these training tasks
are generally trained in parallel using a single 8-card GPU host
cluster (for example, 8 A100/A800/H100/H800), and various high-
performance computing service providers are constantly launching
new solutions to cope with the rapidly growing large model training
and reasoning costs. NVIDIA’s DGX SuperPOD architecture is
composed of 140 8*A100 servers. Microsoft, Meta, NVIDIA, and
Tesla have all used clusters containing thousands of cards built on
the SuperPOD architecture. In addition, there is also a single-node
32GPU solution launched by GigaIO. All of these reflect the rapid
increase in computing requirements for large model training.
As shown in Figure 1, the most basic layer of the SuperPOD
architecture is a SU consisting of 20*A100 and 8 leaf switches, each
of which is connected to each A100. Above the SU is a spine
switch consisting of 10*QM8790 switches, and above them are core
switches consisting of more QM8790s. The connections between
switches meet the fat tree topology. In the example of 140 8*A100
servers in Figure 2, the core switches are divided into two groups,
each of which is connected to half of the spine switches.[6]
At present, large models are still one of the hot research fron-
tiers, and their rapid development is foreseeable. Therefore, the
growth of demand for high-performance computing in the training
and reasoning process of large models is also foreseeable. Just like
other fields that require high-performance computing resources,
security is also an important topic in the process of large model
training, especially those tasks that need to be provided by confiden-
tial computing service providers on the cloud. When the number
of GPUs and hosts involved in the calculation is small, it is not a
problem to worry about these GPUs and hosts remotely proving
to users, and traditional one-to-one solutions can also cope with
it. However, as the number of GPUs and hosts increases, tradi-
tional one-to-one remote proving will consume a lot of resources.
Therefore, an efficient remote proving solution is needed to reduce
the burden of security verification of GPUs and hosts, so that the
high-performance computing resources that are very valuable in
the training process can play a role where they are more needed.
2.2
Swarm Attestation
Swarm attestation is an important branch of remote attestation.
Common remote attestation mechanisms are mainly aimed at ap-
plication scenarios where the initiator of remote attestation and
the confidential computing server correspond one-to-one (in some
cases, a trusted third party will participate in the attestation pro-
cess), and it is difficult to expand to one-to-many or many-to-many
application scenarios, which are almost never encountered in real-
ity. Therefore, some swarm attestation methods for scenarios with
multiple participants have emerged in recent years.
With the development of embedded devices, mobile devices and
their networks and the rise of the Internet of Things, a large amount
of sensitive data related to user privacy is placed in devices with
insufficient computing power. It is more difficult to protect the
security of these devices and data. Many-to-many remote attesta-
tion is particularly important in these fields. This is why swarm
attestation is used in these fields - swarm attestation is used in the
field of the Internet of Things as a global attestation mechanism for
the cluster environment composed of large-scale Internet of Things
devices to verify the integrity of device hardware and software,
thereby defending against possible attacks on a large number of
devices in the Internet of Things.
The swarm attestation mechanism is applied in the field of Inter-
net of Things and embedded systems because it can solve the remote
attestation problem with multiple participants. It can be mainly

divided into two categories: group attestation and distributed attes-
tation:
Group Attestation: There is a centralized verifier in group at-
testation to ultimately verify a large number of devices. In such a
model, the group network can be static. If all devices can partici-
pate in the interaction at the same time, that is, the entire group
is interconnected and will not change during the positive process,
then a tree network can be constructed based on this, in which
the devices have a clear parent-child relationship; if the devices
cannot be online at the same time, then the devices need to com-
plete the attestation protocol independently, and then propagate
the request and results to each other. In this case, there is usually
no clear tree structure, and the nodes are not strictly parent-child
relationships; and if it is assumed that the group is also dynamic
during the attestation, the current method tends to use the con-
sensus technology in remote attestation (which is proposed to be
used in distributed systems to coordinate the various nodes to keep
pace and advance and retreat together, such as blockchains often
use workload for attestation.), let the devices share their knowl-
edge with other devices in advance, and then use the consensus
mechanism between them to coordinate the consensus of the entire
network, so that the common knowledge is consistent, and the
devices interact synchronously during the attestation, but in this
case, the existing schemes usually do not need to build a spanning
tree to collect attestation reports.
Since Asokan et al. proposed the first IoT group attestation
scheme SEDA, which uses spanning trees and recursive calculations
to determine the integrity of the entire group, rather than proving
each device individually as in traditional methods[7], it has contin-
ued to develop; Ambrosin et al. proposed SANA based on SEDA to
improve the security of the scheme through untrusted aggregators
and public verifiability[8]; Dushku et al. proposed SARA, an asyn-
chronous communication protocol for the Internet of Things[9];
Ibrahim et al. proposed SeED, a non-interactive attestation scheme
for denial of service (DoS) attacks[10]; Gong et al. formalized the
sensor node Describe and propose a remote attestation mechanism
that can track nodes in real time[11]; Carpent et al. proposed a new
group attestation metric QoSA and two remote attestation schemes
LISAa and LISAs. LISAs is a synchronous version that uses the
superposition of spanning trees to build the network into a bal-
anced binary tree, while LISAa is an asynchronous version. When
executing attestation, nodes do not build parent-child relationships,
but complete the attestation independently and propagate requests
and results to each other during interaction[12]; Kohnhäuser et
al. proposed SALAD, a dynamic network attestation scheme that
uses self-attestation to propagate and accumulate attestation results
in the group so that the attestation is no longer restricted by the
network topology[13].
Distributed Attestation: There is no traditional centralized ver-
ifier in distributed attestation. Instead, the devices in the network
verify each other to ensure security. The methods used by various
distributed attestation schemes are relatively diverse. Ibrahim et al.
proposed a remote attestation mechanism US-AID for autonomous
devices in a dynamic network, in which devices can attest to each
other and save network snapshots. Autonomous devices in the
protocol need to store their own neighbor attestation results and
judge the network health status based on these results[14]; EDSRA
proposed by Kuang et al. divides large IoT networks into several
clusters based on communication distance and introduces a rep-
utation mechanism to evaluate the previous behavior of devices.
Each attestor needs to obtain attestation from three different neigh-
bors. The cluster head node will check the attestor’s corresponding
evaluation score and report it to the verifier[15]; Ibrahim et al. sub-
sequently proposed a method that can detect malicious devices in
addition to HEALED, a remote attestation mechanism that can also
“repair” infected devices[16]; Visintin et al. proposed a decentral-
ized attestation process SAFEd that allows a pair of IoT devices
to verify their integrity without relying on external verifiers[17];
Abera et al. proposed a protocol DIAT that authenticates the com-
munication data exchanged between two devices together with the
control flow attestation of the software modules involved in data
generation to ensure the security of the interaction between the
two devices[18]; Kohnhauser et al. proposed a protocol PASTA that
allows low-end embedded provers to collaborate periodically to
generate timestamped “tokens”[19].

Model DesiGnation
3.1
System Composition
The system consists of users, i.e. verifiers, and a large number of
GPU clusters, i.e. provers, who may be vulnerable to attacks by
potential attackers.
Each host in the cluster should have:
• A static non-volatile write-safe memory area for storing code
segments (code and data).
• Secure storage of keys that can only be accessed when the
code in the secure memory area is executed.
• The code in protected memory is secure and does not leak
any information except the final result. They constitute the
root of trust of the device.
3.2
Threat Model
Assume that a malicious attacker has the following capabilities:
1) Attacker can eavesdrop, insert or modify all information ex-
changed between devices.
2) Attacker can control the device memory and modify the mem-
ory area on the platform before authentication.
3) Attacker can perform replay attacks, pre-calculate the memory
to be traversed, perform memory replacement attacks, etc.
4) Attacker cannot modify the hardware device during authenti-
cation.
5) Attacker cannot forge signatures.
6) Attacker cannot launch a DDoS attack on the entire network
scale.
We have the following security assumptions:
1) The verifier knows the hardware and software configuration
of each management node (considering that the hosts are homoge-
neous, in fact, the verifier only needs to know the hardware and
software configuration of a certain host).
2) The clock of the device is synchronized with the confidential
computing service provider and the verifier, and will not be attacked
by A.
3) Most of the homogeneous hosts are trustworthy, and only a
few are attacked.
4) The confidential computing service provider is trustworthy,
and all cryptographic functions are secure.
5) When performing the initial key exchange in the offline phase,
it is assumed that there is a secure channel between any two nodes.
6) The devices in the cluster can be moved dynamically, but
during the authentication period, the cluster is static.
For the main research content introduced in the previous article,
only by adopting appropriate research methods and appropriate
technical routes can it be easier to produce research results and re-
duce the time and energy wasted in the research process. Therefore,
the research methods and technical routes planned to be adopted
in this topic are as follows.
3.3
Protocol Designation
In the multi-GPU multi-host cluster used for large model training,
quite a few hosts are actually likely to be homogeneous, that is,
their software and hardware configurations are the same, and the
large model training process formally distributes the work to a
large number of such homogeneous hosts in the cluster for parallel
computing.
Considering the characteristics of the hosts in the above cluster,
although it is more efficient to add these hosts to the cluster one
by one and verify them than to verify them one by one, the results
are similar. Grouping homogeneous hosts, each group contains
a management host to verify other hosts in the group, and then
verifying the management hosts will improve the efficiency a lot. In
the case of a large number of hosts, each group with a management
host can continue to be grouped, thus forming a multi-layer tree
structure with the user who needs to verify these hosts as the
root, and each node is responsible for verifying its own subtree
and passing the verification results upward, and finally completing
the verification of the entire tree. Such a structure also brings an
advantage, that is, it is possible to search down the tree to locate
those unsafe hosts that cannot pass the verification.
In addition, since service providers that provide confidential
computing services on the cloud may need to dynamically allocate
resources and change the allocated resources in some cases, adding
and deleting nodes in the tree structure can also meet the needs of
service providers, thereby ensuring the scalability of the cluster.
Our protocol is divided into two stages: offline and online.
1) Offline Stage: The offline phase is responsible for initializing
and updating the hosts in the cluster.
Specifically, during the initialization phase, the confidential com-
puting service provider will configure the signature key pair (signed
by the confidential computing service provider) and communication
key of each host, and provide the public key of the user (verifier)
to each host. At the same time, during this phase, the confidential
computing service provider also needs to group the hosts to form a
tree structure required for verification, and the root node of the tree
structure is responsible for directly interacting with the verifier.
The number and depth of the tree branches should ensure that the
message propagates as quickly as possible. Taking a cluster of 140
8*A100 servers as an example, forming a binary tree can allow in-
formation to propagate faster on the tree until the leaf node. After
the tree structure is generated, each node needs to exchange keys
with adjacent nodes.
The information that each host needs to update can be divided
into the addition of new hosts and the update of neighboring nodes.
When a new host is added to the cluster, the confidential computing
service provider needs to assign a key pair and the user’s public
key to it. And put this new device into the tree structure, and then
let it exchange keys with its neighboring nodes according to the
position of the node in the tree structure.
As for the update within the tree structure, each node can send
information to its subtree at regular intervals to update the status
of the nodes in the subtree of the node, and pass its own results
upward to its parent node. Ultimately, the data of all nodes will be
gathered at the root node of the tree structure.
2) Online Stage: The online stage is responsible for completing
remote attestation and finding possible attacked hosts.
In the online phase, when the verifier wants to verify the trusted
state of the cluster, it needs to first pass through the root node of
the book transfer structure. This node needs to verify each other
with the verifier, which can defend against DOS attacks to a certain
extent. Once the verification is passed, the root node can pass the

remote attestation requirement to its subtree, and the root node of
each subtree, that is, the management node of a group of hosts, will
also pass this request down until it reaches a leaf node. Each leaf
node will complete remote verification with its parent node, pass
this result upward, and also perform remote verification with the
parent node. When this process is completed, the conclusion of the
remote verification will reach the root node of the tree structure,
and according to the attestation results passed up step by step, it
can also be determined which node has a problem.
In the above process, verification can be roughly divided into
two categories: mutual authentication between the user and the
root node of the tree structure, and authentication between nodes
within the tree structure.
Considering the situation between nodes within the tree struc-
ture, the nodes can be divided into two categories: management
nodes and other nodes. The management node is the root node
of a subtree, and the other nodes are other nodes of the subtree.
Authentication starts from the leaves of the tree structure and then
goes up step by step. The subtree that has been authenticated can be
regarded as a ”leaf” node. When authenticating, the management
node will actively send a request:
• Send request: The management node sends an encrypted
verification request to detect the status of the sub-device
node at a fixed interval (this time is less than the remote
verification interval). The verification request should contain
at least a random data and an increasing serial number and
the host’s globally unique ID, and then wait for the reply
of other nodes. The waiting time should be limited, and
timeout should be considered a failure. Since the entire host
cluster is controlled by the confidential computing service
provider, this time limit is unlikely to be affected by the
network environment.
• Wait: The management node waits for the verification infor-
mation sent back by other nodes. If the timer setting time
is not exceeded when the information is received, it is con-
sidered that the authentication has failed and directly enters
the recording stage.
• Record: If the received message is a reply from other nodes,
the management node needs to check the signature of the
received information and decrypt it. If the serial number in
the information is consistent with the serial number sent by
the management node, the checksum in the information is
recorded and the node ID contained in the information is
placed in the set of replied nodes. If all other nodes have
replied, the verification stage is entered, otherwise it returns
to the waiting stage.
Verification: In this phase, the management node compares the
checksums of all nodes recorded in the recording phase. Nodes with
checksums different from the majority of nodes will be considered
as authentication failures and added to the verification failure sub-
device set. Otherwise, the node will be added to the verification
success sub-device set and its remote attestation conclusion will be
adopted.
In this process, other nodes will follow the following steps:
• Wait: Wait for the verification request from the management
node, and enter the verification phase after receiving the
request.
• Verification: After receiving the message from the manage-
ment node, check the signature of the verification request
sent by the management node and decrypt to obtain the
serial number and random data, and then verify whether
the serial number of the request is legal, that is, the serial
number must be greater than the serial number used in the
previous verification phase stored by the child device node.
After passing the verification, the local authentication of the
8 GPUs under the host is started, and their authentication
results are saved. Then, the node fills the blank memory
with random numbers, and then calculates the checksum of
the memory and the received random data, and enters the
response phase. The interaction of these nodes is shown in
Figure 2.
When a management node passes the verification, it will partici-
pate in the authentication of its parent node as other nodes until
the management node has no parent node, that is, it reaches the
root of the tree structure. At this time, the root of the tree structure
needs to interact with the user. The authentication process is simi-
lar to the authentication of the management node. When the user
initiates the authentication, the authentication process will start:
• Send request: The user sends an encrypted verification re-
quest to the root node of the tree structure to detect the
status of all device nodes. The verification request contains a
random number that will be used to calculate the checksum
and an increasing sequence number, and then sets the timer
to enter the waiting stage. The same is true for the authenti-
cation process between nodes. The waiting time should be
limited, and the timeout should be considered a failure.
• Wait: Wait for the verification information sent back by
other nodes. If the timer setting is not exceeded when the in-
formation is received, it is considered that the authentication
has failed and directly enters the verification stage.
• Verification: After receiving the reply message from the
root node, check the signature of the received information
and decrypt it. If the sequence number in the information
is consistent with the sequence number sent by the user,
the corresponding checksum is calculated based on the re-
ceived random data and compared with the checksum in the
information. If the comparison results are consistent, the
authentication is considered successful.
After receiving a request from the user, the root node of the tree
structure should also follow the steps:
• Wait: Wait for the remote authentication request and related
information sent by the user. After receiving the authentica-
tion request sent by the user, the verification phase will be
entered.
• Verification: First, it is necessary to determine whether the
signature of the received request is correct. If it is correct,
decrypt the information and obtain the serial number and
random number from the information. Then verify the serial
number of the request information. It must be greater than
the serial number used in the previous verification phase

stored by the management node to be considered as verified.
After passing the verification, if the root node has received
the authentication information of other nodes at this time
and has not initiated a new round of authentication, the
authentication information will be sent directly to the user.
Otherwise, the root node needs to send an authentication re-
quest to its child node, which is the process described above,
and then forward the result to the user after the authentica-
tion is completed.
In normal times (Figure 3), the heartbeat protocol can be used
regularly inside the tree structure to regularly determine the status
of adjacent nodes. Here, only a simple challenge-response test is
needed. If a node is found to be untrustworthy, the node where the
problem is found is used as the root, and the mentality protocol is
run on the child nodes of the node to confirm the status, and the
information is passed upward.
After receiving the transmitted information, the verifier can
determine which hosts in the cluster are trustworthy, and the confi-
dential computing service provider can also adjust the tree structure
according to the host situation.
When a host fails to authenticate (Figure 4), if it is a leaf node,
it means that it is untrustworthy. Otherwise, after all nodes are
authenticated, the child nodes of the node need to be authenticated
(here, since the information provided by the untrustworthy node
Figure 4: Attestation of the tree structure, a node is unsafe.
cannot be used, its child nodes are also considered untrustworthy).
At this time, the untrustworthy parent nodes should be excluded,
and the remaining nodes should be reorganized into a tree structure.
The new root node contacts the verifier and uses the protocol to
authenticate the new tree structure.
After the initial authentication is completed, the verifier should
successfully verify the trustworthiness of a batch of GPU clusters
that form a tree or forest structure and can start using them.
4
Experiments and Analysis
4.1
Experimentation and Evaluation
Assuming that the time for a single device to complete the attes-
tation is 푡, since our method uses a tree structure to prove, the
time consumption will be at the 푂(푙표푔(푡)) level, while the ordinary
one-to-one attestation method is at the 푂(푡) level.
In order to verify the effectiveness of our idea, we simulated it
on a Laptop with a processor i5-8300H and 8.00 GB of RAM. In this
simulation, we simply simulated two different remote attestation
schemes, one of which is our scheme, and the other is a simple
scheme that verifies all nodes one by one. Since the protocols
used in the two simulations are simple versions implemented by

performance of the protocol will decrease. In addition, since our
protocol has a situation where the remote attestation of some nodes
depends on other nodes, the position of the attacked node in the
tree structure will also affect its impact on the performance of the
protocol.
However, when there is a fixed number of nodes under attack,
the performance of our protocol is still better than simply scaling
up the one-to-one remote attestation protocol, as shown in Figure

4.2
Security Analysis
According to the preliminarily designed process, consider the pos-
sible threats and conduct a simple security analysis.
1) Forgery Attack: If attacker A constructs a message and its
signature value without knowing the key, the signature forged by A
cannot be verified because the hosts in the cluster have shared the
key in advance during the offline phase, thus achieving the effect
of defending against forgery attacks.
When the management node is isomorphic with other nodes,
the management node cannot use the verification information sent
by other nodes because the random number generation function
is stored in the secure memory area and cannot be accessed by
external programs. This makes the work of generating random
numbers only completed by the authentication code, and the ran-
dom numbers generated each time are different, that is, the random
number used by the management node to calculate the checksum
is different from the random number used by the child node of the
management node, so A cannot forge random numbers.
Even if A has affected a host that serves as a management node
through a malicious program and let it pass its own random number
to the child node, this process will also bring time delays.
2) Replay Attack: A transmits previously authenticated data to
the user or management node. Since random numbers are intro-
duced during verification, A cannot calculate the content required
for the verification process in advance. The existence of the serial
number prevents A from directly intercepting old messages and
sending them to the user or nodes in the tree structure to pass the
verification, thus defending against replay attacks.
3) Memory Copy or Replacement Attack: If A copies the memory
to a blank area, and when verifying the memory, the attack is carried
out by modifying the program counter or data pointer through a
malicious program, then the step of filling the blank memory with
random numbers will make it impossible for A to store the attack
code, thereby resisting A’s attack.
4) Proxy Attack: Assuming that A uses a faster remote device
proxy to check and calculate, then A’s remote device will not be
able to encrypt and sign correctly because it cannot obtain the real
key, and thus cannot attack.
5) Memory Compression Attack: If A obtains available free mem-
ory by compressing the memory through a malicious program, and
then decompresses it in real time during the attestation, then set-
ting event limits and filling the memory with random numbers can
defend to a certain extent.
6) Collusion Attack: If A uses two devices to attack in series,
when the collusion attack occurs on the child node, because the
results sent are protected by encrypted signatures, even if they
are sent to another malicious node, the malicious node will fail
to decrypt due to lack of keys, and thus the collusion cannot be
completed.
When the collusion attack occurs between management nodes,
if the malicious node controlled by A pre-transmits the random
number to the next node, so that the next node can pre-calculate,
then by placing the mechanism for generating random numbers
in the secure memory area, ensuring that only the authentication
code can call it, so that the random number cannot be generated in
advance, this collusion attack can be defended.
7) Confidentiality Guarantee: Since the design adopts the method
of encrypting information and assumes that the cryptographic
function used is secure, even if A intercepts the information, it
cannot obtain the message content, thereby achieving the purpose
of preventing eavesdropping.
8) Availability Guarantee: After a node is missing and attacked
and is no longer secure, a mechanism for reorganizing the affected
part of the tree structure is introduced so that the missing node
does not affect the transmission of other nodes to ensure the further
operation of the protocol.
In addition, since users need to be authenticated at the root node
of the tree structure, DOS attacks can be defended to a certain
extent.
5
Conclusion
Currently, this solution is still in a relatively preliminary stage. It
has certain advantages over direct one-to-one attestation, but it
has not yet been optimized specifically for GPU attestation. There-
fore, we will continue to optimize our solution for specific GPU
attestation environments in the future.

Abstract: With the rapid development of artificial intelligence and machine learning in recent years, their complexity has also increased rapidly, and therefore the demand for high-performance computing has also increased rapidly. The traditional way of distributing training and inference work to a large number of servers will further increase the complexity of these tasks and slow down the process, which is particularly detrimental to those tasks that are time-sensitive. To solve these problems, many designs have emerged that integrate a large number of GPUs together, such as the DGX SuperPOD architecture launched by NVIDIA. However, as the number of GPUs in a server increases, security issues also arise. It is obviously too cumbersome to directly verify each GPU one by one. Therefore, we can refer to the swarm attestation mechanism of IoT devices and design a new remote attestation protocol based on structures such as SuperPOD that integrate a large number of GPUs together, so that users can quickly verify the security of a large number of GPUs in the SuperPOD structure, thereby improving the efficiency of remote attestation. This paper introduces the swarm attestation mechanism of the Internet of Things into the remote attestation of a multi-GPU cluster with a SuperPOD structure, proposes a remote attestation protocol based on the swarm attestation mechanism, and verifies in simulation that it is more efficient than simply expanding the ordinary one-to-one GPU remote attestation mechanism. At the same time, its analysis shows that the scheme can resist attacks such as forgery and replay.
